slides.heading: Filariasis
slides.subtitle: A chronic, disfiguring parasitic disease of the lymphatic system.

slides.heading: Overview
bullets: Often progresses to a chronic, debilitating, disfiguring disease (symptoms unnoticed early).
High rates in Region V (Bicol), VIII (Samar, Leyte), and XI (Davao).
Causative agents: Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi.
Transmitted by infected female mosquitoes (Aedes, Anopheles, Mansonia).
Larvae travel via bloodstream and lodge in lymphatic vessels/glands, maturing into adults.

terms.definition: Microfilaria circulate in peripheral blood at night (10 PM–2 AM).
Microfilaria circulate in greater concentration during the daytime.

slides.heading: Clinical Stages
rows: Filarial fever & lymphatic inflammation (up to 10×/yr, abates in ~7 days); lymphadenitis, lymphangitis
Hydrocele (scrotal swelling), lymphedema, elephantiasis (thickened skin of extremities)

slides.heading: Management
bullets: Specific: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 6 mg/kg in divided doses for 12 consecutive days; Ivermectin (Mectizan).
DEC: take immediately after meals; prolonged use may cause vision loss, night blindness, tunnel vision.
Ivermectin: single dose with a full glass of water on an empty stomach; NOT for asthma patients.
Supportive: paracetamol, antihistamine (for DEC allergy), vitamin B complex, limb elevation, elastic stockings.

slides.heading: Key Takeaways
bullets: Wuchereria bancrofti / Brugia malayi → lymphatic filariasis.
Nocturnal microfilaria peak 10 PM–2 AM (key for blood smear timing).
Treat with DEC (after meals) ± ivermectin (empty stomach, not in asthma).
